content.title: Withdrawal of Submission
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their time and valuable feedback. We are glad that the reviewers recognize the problem as important (sbeG), our experiments extensive (sbeG, 4Tiq, uuY2, NHLb), and the paper as being clearly written and easy to follow (sbeG, 4Tiq, uuY2, NHLb). 

We also appreciate the improvements to the paper that the reviewers have suggested, such as better motivation and assumptions for the selection of augmenations $q(x’|x)$ (sbeG, 4Tiq, NHLb), theoretical analysis on the properties of our complexity measure (sbeG, NHLb), and stronger comparison to existing methods (sbeG, 4Tiq, NHLb). Given the limited time window, we have decided to withdraw the paper, and will work on these experimental improvements for a future submission.

Here, we would like to clarify several comments regarding the conceptual components of the paper.

1. **Dismissal of prior work [1]** [sbeG]

We argue that the prior work of [1] is sufficiently different from ours due to the weight tuning required on each dataset tested as well as their need for labeled test data. For practitioners, our measure can be used even when high quality labelled data may not be available.

2. **The use of augmentation during training rather than as a complexity measure** [4Tiq]

We argue that these two considerations are orthogonal. Training with data augmentation should improve generalization, but precisely characterizing this generalization in unknown distributions is still important. We plan to add additional results showing that our method works even when models are trained with the same augmentation method used to measure smoothness with respect to.

3. **the underlying data manifold in text and images** [NHLb]

We do not assume that these manifolds are the same. Although the way that we calculate smoothness is the same between text and images, the augmentations $q(x’|x)$ used are different, and thus the representation space with respect to which we measure smoothness is different.

References:
[1]: https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.06459

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a model free notion of "manifold smoothness", and presents a series of numerical experiments demonstrating that this metric is correlated with the in-domain and out-of-domain generalization capabilities of a variety of deep learning models in image classification, sentiment analysis, and natural language interpretation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- The problem addressed in the paper---understanding the factors affecting [OOD] generalization---is important and timely.
- The idea of utilizing manifolds to model the data domain and of relating the smoothness of this manifold with model generalization is well-motivated.
- The paper is very well written and the numerical experiments are extensive.

Weaknessess:

- The paper introduces a notion of manifold smoothness but the manifold itself, and in particular the neighborhoods $N_\mathcal{M}$ and the conditional distributions $q(x'|x)$, are not formally defined. There is no manifold/differential geometry formalism. Specific comments:
  - How can one be sure that the data augmentation techniques used to define $q(x'|x)$ in Sec. 4.2. correspond to translations/diffeomorphisms over the manifold? The experiments themselves suggest that "the choice of neighborhood becomes much more important as we move farther from the training domain" (last sentence of Sec. 5.2), however, the paper offers no insight on how to choose these neighborhoods, and uses rather arbitrary data augmentation techniques that do not have any clear connections with manifolds and that are not described in detail in the paper.
  - Similarly, how do you know, in the case of images, that patch erasing and flip and crops "poorly reflect the true manifold"? (paragraph **Image Classification** of Sec. 5.1)
  - It is not clear whether $x$ itself is included in the definition of neighborhood in equation (1).
- Important information is missing in the numerical experiments:
  - What's the MAE in Tables  2a and 2b?
  - Fig. 3b is puzzling. When the number of generated samples is 1, if $x$ is included in the computation of the smoothness, $\mu$ is either $0.5$ or $1$. It's strange that the correlation remains constant as the number of samples grows. It'd also be interesting to see a few values of $\mu$ and of the MAE for this experiment.
  - The neighborhood size in Fig 3b is not specified.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a metric for quantifying model generalization, i.e. its performance on previously unseen data. The metric is defined as the sensitivity of the model predictions to data augmentations that the predictions must be invariant to (e.g. erasing a small random patch in an image). Authors test how predictive the proposed metric is of model's generalization on OOD data.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The metric and motivation behind it are presented clearly and in great detail.
- Extensive experiments with a wide variety of models and datasets. Extensive experimental detail.

Weaknesses/Questions:
- Using a measure of model invariance to estimate its generalization ability is of limited novelty. [1] (cited in the paper) already showed that this can work well. This prior method is being dismissed way too quickly in the discussion due to differing details in the metrics formulation. At the very least, it should be compared to in the experiments, which would evidence the advantage of the proposed method. In addition, [2] consider methods along similar lines. There is likely more work in the adversarial learning community (assuming we want models to be invariant to low-magnitude noise) that I am not aware of.
- More discussion of how exactly to interpret the number and apply the metric in practice would make the paper more useful to practitioners.
- The method assumes that we know (and can implement) the required augmentation methods. If this is the case, why don't we simply use these augmentation methods to _improve_ the generalization of the model? In other words, if we want to use this metric, we can't apply these augmentation methods to the training data anymore.
- Experiments suggest the metric is sensitive to the choice of the augmentation methods. This makes me doubt that the metric would be useful for data where defining the augmentation methods is difficult (e.g. tabular data).

References:
- \[1\]: https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.06459
- \[2\]: https://openreview.net/forum?id=d87PBvj7LA7
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Good clarity, quality and reproducibility: the proposed metric and experiments are introduced and discussed in great detail. Novelty is limited: see the discussion above.
content.summary_of_the_review: Unfortunately, I don't see enough novelty in the paper to recommend it for acceptance. Prior work has already shown that using invariance as a proxy for generalization is worthwhile. The (arguably minor) differences between the prior and the proposed metrics are not discussed in sufficient detail, and are not carefully evaluated.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a very simple metric to estimate the generalization properties of a model that, differently from existing metrics, positively correlates with the generalization performance. The metric is extremely simple to implement, although it requires the definition of an augmentation strategy in order to be measured, and this might relatively limit its applicability. The authors perform extensive experiments to evaluate the goodness of the metric.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The proposed method is simple and seems to be pretty effective
- The bibliography is extensive, well curated and discussed
- The limitations are tackled and shown to the reader, but are negligible given the almost total uselessness of other complexity measures 

Weaknesses:
- The presentation can be improved in the following aspects: (1) you could probably discuss more explicitly what the purpose of each of your metrics is (especially ID, Micro/Macro/Arch tau), from the experiments conclusions and reasoning a bit one can infer why you propose them, but it would be nice to immediately understand why you introduce them and what aspect of the problem you would like to poke, (2) you introduce the symbol $g_{io}^k$ without defining it and then you give a definition in the following paragraph. It was a bit confusing, you could at least quickly mention you will define the quantity later and what's its purpose (I thought I had missed something). (3) It could help being a bit more bullet-pointy about the experiments and conclusions (especially when multiple metrics need to be checked to draw a conclusion), so that the results and the variety of experiments you perform immediately stand out. 
- It could be nice showing it scales to imagenet, mostly because of the large availability of OOD datasets and the complexity of having smooth predictions with a much higher number of classes. 


Additional interesting experiments that could make the paper stronger:
- Q1: The authors of [1] tried to use spectral complexity measures in the attempt of determining whether Transformers and CNNs are qualitatively different, and the complexity and robustness of their feature space could be captured with known complexity measures. The results were disappointing. Would it be possible to use your metric to solve the issue they expose? Showing that your metric can "sort" models based on their generalization capacities across classes of models with significantly different inductive biases might be really useful, and it would improve the impact of your paper and be definitely remarkable.
- Q2: as already discussed by the authors, the augmentation type plays an important role. Unrealistic augmentations might have an adverse effect. SInce there are extremely rich strategies of augmentations for vision, could you provide a few more analyses on this aspect?

[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.11347

content.summary_of_the_paper: The work proposes a simple way to estimate generalisation accuracy based on the label purity of perturbed data. More specifically, they utilise data augmentations to generate sample points in the neighbourhood and measure the fraction of the samples classified into the majority predicted class. Through the experiments, the authors argue that their proposed smoothness measure is linearly correlated with the actual OOD generalisation accuracy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 

The proposed method is clearly explained and the paper structure is easy to follow. The paper includes sufficient experiments to demonstrate the strong correlation between their proposed smoothness measure and OOD generalisation accuracy.  

Weakness: 

The proposed smooth measure is very simple, almost elementary. There is insufficient theoretical justification for this simple measure to work in diverse input formats. It would be good to clarify the assumptions made for the underlying data manifold that helps to justify the proposed smoothness measure. E.g. How is the distance (r) defined on the manifold? Also are there any properties of smoothness that the proposed measure satisfies? 

It would be good for the authors to clarify why the proposed data augmentation methods are likely to generate neighbourhood samples in the underlying manifold. 

Also it would be good to include a discussion on how the proposed smoothness measure may differ across multiple modalities (image, text). Since the same smoothness measure is used across different modalities, do the authors assume the underlying data manifold to be the same?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well structured and some ideas are clearly articulated. The contributions are rather trivial. The idea is not very novel; It seems to be a simplification of this paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.06061). Many parts of the experimental settings are questionable, in particular, there are no clear assumptions on what types of OOD distribution the paper is trying to address.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed solution is very simple and may have been subsumed by prior studies (particularly https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.06061). It also does not explain why some augmentations can outperform others and how these augmented samples generate local neighbourhoods on the manifold as the authors claim.

content.title: Predicting Out-of-Domain Generalization with Local Manifold Smoothness
content.TL;DR: Local manifold smoothness is a novel complexity measure that can be used to predict generalization even on out-of-domain test sets without labels.
content.abstract: Understanding how machine learning models generalize to new environments is a critical part of their safe deployment. Recent work has proposed a variety of complexity measures that directly predict or theoretically bound the generalization capacity of a model. However, these methods rely on a strong set of assumptions that in practice are not always satisfied. Motivated by the limited settings in which existing measures can be applied, we propose a novel complexity measure based on the local manifold smoothness of a classifier. We define local manifold smoothness as a classifier's output sensitivity to perturbations in the manifold neighborhood around a given test point. Intuitively, a classifier that is less sensitive to these perturbations should generalize better. To estimate smoothness we sample points using data augmentation and measure the fraction of these points classified into the majority class. Our method only requires selecting a data augmentation method and makes no other assumptions about the model or data distributions, meaning it can be applied even in out-of-domain (OOD) settings where existing methods cannot. In experiments on robustness benchmarks in image classification, sentiment analysis, and natural language inference, we demonstrate a strong and robust correlation between our manifold smoothness measure and actual OOD generalization on over 4,000 models evaluated on over 100 train/test domain pairs.
